weak: Not in general, and in the cases I have tested, not measurably. Adding 800 and then 3,000 tokens of irrelevant house rules to a classifier did not change accuracy on 60 tickets with Haiku 4.5. I have seen one practitioner write-up, from an excerpt only, reporting that a 4,675-token production prompt underperformed a 128-token one, and my guess is that the cause was contradictory rules in that prompt rather than length, though I have not tested that myself. So I read a long prompt for conflicts and ablate sections before I assume length is the problem. The cost side is different: input tokens are billed on every call, so a prompt that adds nothing to quality is pure spend, and I would cut it on cost grounds even when accuracy is flat.

Long context wins when the knowledge is small, queried often and cacheable. My handbook of 160 short clauses ran at 7,581 input tokens a query against 249 for retrieval at k of 4, so an uncached read was roughly 30 times the cost. With a prompt cache the read drops to about a tenth, and below some size the index is not worth building at all. I would compute the crossover from the knowledge base size, the query rate and the cache hit rate, and I would choose retrieval for anything that changes daily. Once the cached long-context setup was live, the monthly bill fell from 412 dollars to 96, and the invoice reconciled to the token counts, so the saving is real.

Because a residual that's labelled and carried forward is more honest than a total that's been forced to balance. If the unexplained amount is 1.9 percent, I'd show it as its own line with a note on what we've ruled out so far, rather than spreading it across cost centres. Reconciling the metered total back to the invoice is what proves the books close, and once they do, the residual is just a known gap we're tracking. A line that's allowed to shrink over time tells the team the meter is being watched.

By how often requests need it. If the block applies to nearly every request, it goes in the cached prefix, since the cache pays for itself across all those calls. If it applies to one request in five or fewer, I take it out of the prefix and load it only when an early step identifies the intent, or pull it through retrieval. That converts a cost paid on every call into one paid on some calls, in exchange for a lookup or a classification call. Before I count the saving, I check the cost of that lookup and the retrieval miss rate, and I compare the result against the cached-prefix baseline for the same traffic.

I work it out from the numbers rather than trusting a rule of thumb. Cost per thousand requests is the hourly price divided by requests served per hour at the utilisation I expect. On my assumed $2.50 an hour and 50 requests a second the cost is $0.014 per thousand at full load and $0.69 at 2 percent, which is above the API's price. The sources I read put the break-even near 30 percent. I would start by measuring average and peak demand over a month, then size the instance so the peak is covered and the average sits above that threshold. Smoothing the load with batching and queueing is part of the plan, since it lifts the effective utilisation without adding hardware. Once it is running I would track cost per thousand requests weekly against the API equivalent, and I would expect the self-hosted route to beat the API by a wide margin once utilisation holds above break-even.

The meter first, then the owners, then the forecast, then the levers. Before I touch anything I want every token, call and GPU-hour tagged to a team, a model and a feature, so the bill can be read by the thing that spent it. Once the meter exists, I name an owner for each line of spend and each model deployment, because a cost nobody answers for will never move. The forecast comes next, built from usage trends per feature, so we see the month-end number before it arrives. Only then do the levers: routing easy requests to smaller models, caching repeated prompts, trimming context, and batching anything that doesn't need a real-time answer. The first saving I'd book is the one where total spend falls against last quarter's invoice, since that is the number finance will trust. And in the first month I'd agree in writing who may stop a runaway agent without asking, so nobody has to wait for a meeting while the spend climbs. I'd also put the price table under the same ownership as the canary that checks it, so a silent vendor price change gets caught the day it happens.

Price it on the mean run cost plus a margin, since that is what the finance model needs to recover. Take the total monthly spend on agent runs, divide by the number of completed runs, and add a markup that covers the platform overhead and a target gross margin of around 60 percent. Quote that per-run rate as a flat fee so the customer can forecast their bill, and let the usage tiers absorb the heavier runs over time. I would validate the rate by checking that the blended revenue per run covers the blended cost per run across the last quarter, and I would revisit it whenever the model version or the prompt changes, since that is what moves cost. The main thing to avoid is pricing per token, because the customer cannot predict token counts and will push back on the invoice.

The most likely cause is a producer change that renamed or moved the input token field, while the usage model reads only the fields it expects and falls back to a default when a field is missing. The schema passes because the reader never complains about absent keys, so zero flows into the cost totals without any error. I reproduced this on real records: the lenient model returned 0 input tokens where the true count was 613, and nothing in the pipeline flagged it.

Prevention has three layers. First, the schema rejects unknown fields and carries an explicit version, so a renamed field fails loudly at ingestion instead of defaulting quietly. Second, the gateway quarantines any record that fails validation, attaching a reason and a named owner, and alerts when the quarantine share crosses a threshold, so a spike in failures is visible within the hour. Third, producer teams run the same validator in their test environment, and we ask for it on the day of any change that touches usage events. Quarantine rates are reviewed weekly against the baseline from the prior month, so drift is caught before it reaches the monthly invoice reconciliation.

For a third-party producer we do not control, the checks have to live in the warehouse load itself, since we cannot rely on their test environment. There, a load that drops below a row-count or token-volume floor halts and pages the on-call owner rather than writing zeros into the cost table.

I start by pulling yesterday's Meter records and grouping them by session, then sorting by cost before I touch any settings. Nine sessions at the top of Fieldstone's illustrative Wednesday table account for about 3.2 percent of the day's spend, and the longest one ran 163 steps against a cap of eight. That suggests the spike is concentrated in a tail rather than spread across the middle, so switching models would likely have changed nothing. I open the longest trace, find the repeated call and the error it keeps hitting, and then check what was supposed to stop it. In this case the cap lived inside the agent framework and nothing enforced it at the gateway. What I change is the enforcement point: a step limit and a spend limit checked before each call, plus an alert that fires on the third repeated identical tool call. I leave the model, the prompt and the traffic forecast alone that day. A true volume increase is a different case: if the session table has the same shape at a larger size, the answer is a forecast revision, not a guardrail.

Send it to more people and make it impossible to miss. A showback report that lands in forty inboxes with a clear breakdown by team, model and prompt gives every stakeholder visibility, and visibility is what drives behavior change. In my composed example we rolled it out company-wide and tracked open rates and forwarded links as the adoption signal. Once people can see their own spend next to everyone else's, the pressure to act comes on its own. I track engagement each month and if the report is opened and shared, I count that as a success, and I would only rethink the format if engagement dropped.

I measure it against a human-labelled held-out set and against the teacher's own self-agreement, and I read both. In the paper I read, the student agreed with recorded decisions at 0.913 against a teacher self-agreement of 0.727, and a blinded human sided with the student in 48 of 77 disagreements. I would confirm the student clears the teacher's agreement level on the same held-out set before anything ships. Once it does, I would run the A/B in production on a traffic slice and compare cost per outcome, with the approval rate and the human review queue as the main signals. I would also set a fallback to the larger model for low-confidence cases, and watch the monthly bill to confirm the savings hold as volume grows.

I would move any call where no one is waiting on the response, the requests are independent of each other, and a late answer is still useful to the business. Nightly scoring of closed conversations, offline evaluation runs, bulk catalogue descriptions and embedding refreshes all qualify. Agent loops do not, because each step depends on the output of the previous one. I would confirm the split from a cost record that tags every call with its latency class, so the batchable share is measured rather than guessed. Once tagged, I would move the batchable volume first and report the saving against the prior month's spend on the same tagged workloads.

We'd know a limit is working if the stops it triggers are the right ones and the spend it protects is clearly lower. I'd track three things: how often runs hit the limit, how much spend sits inside those runs, and how far past the limit they go before stopping. If a limit fires on 40 percent of runs, the price is set wrong. If it never fires, it's either set too high to matter or it's guarding nothing real. I'd also log the stop reason for every run, so a cap hit, a circuit-breaker trip and a manual kill don't get lumped together, because each points to a different fix. Finally I'd compare total monthly spend against the prior month to confirm the limit actually reduced cost.

The per-run ceiling in the agent loop, because that is the only place that sees actual usage and can end a run while money is being spent. User, team and global limits in the gateway, because that is where the tags live and the check does not depend on the agent code. The provider's hard limit as a final backstop. A prompt instruction is a nudge and not a control, so I would never rely on it for spend.

One ledger with a state for each saving: identified, committed, or realised. Each entry gets a baseline and the interaction with other levers stated. In my lab, caching saved 87 percent and retrieval 95.8 percent, both against the same baseline, and the two did not add. Caching was applied first, so retrieval was measured against the cached path. I would credit the second lever only with its marginal saving, and reconcile the ledger total to the invoice each month.

I tell her no, and I tell her the reason we didn't catch it: a $212 session against a median of nine cents is a clear outlier, and nine sessions like it made up 3.2 percent of that day's spend. Then I separate the claims so she doesn't have to hold them all at once. The dollars are small against the month. The control gap is large, because the step limit existed in the prompt template but was never enforced at the metering layer where the money is actually spent. And the fix is cheap: a per-session ceiling checked at the meter, which costs a few engineering days and requires no model change. I give her the metric that will show it worked: sessions over twenty steps per week should fall to zero, and the cost of the top one percent of sessions should drop as a share of total spend. We ship the ceiling this sprint and I report the savings against last month's run rate, which will show the loop cost removed at roughly $40k a month. I'd still flag one boundary: a product where long sessions are the point, such as a research agent, needs a ceiling set from the paid outcome rather than a step count, and I'd want that conversation with product before we roll the same rule there.

The cost per emitted response dropping 20 percent while cost per benefited response stays flat means the two numbers are measuring different things, and the gap between them is where the story is. Most likely the model is emitting more responses per unit of benefit, or the benefit rate fell as the cheaper responses got worse. I would pull the accept rate, the recontact rate and the response count per conversation for both quarters. If responses per conversation rose, the agent may be splitting its answers or asking more clarifying questions, which lowers the per-response cost without helping anyone. If the accept rate fell, a cheaper configuration is degrading quality. I would report the benefited number as the headline, show the emitted one as a diagnostic, and not claim the 20 percent as a saving. The boundary is a single-call product, where one response is one task and the two series should move together. A divergence there points to a measurement problem rather than a behavior change.

When a cache hit happens, there is no provider usage block, so the record has to be written by whatever cache layer served the request. I add a cache field with values none, provider-prefix, exact and semantic, plus a hit or miss outcome. For semantic hits I also store the similarity score and the ID of the entry that was served, so a bad match can be traced later. The avoided cost goes into its own estimated field and is kept out of the billed spend total. Cost per outcome is then reported per cache layer as well as overall, because without that split, tasks that were cheap because they were cached get mixed up with tasks that were cheap because they were easy.

I would use a published rule of thumb, such as a minimum multiple of cost to price, as a prompt to check my own table, not as a target. These rules come from assumptions I cannot see, such as the task mix, the cache hit rate, and the share of enterprise seats, so a number that held for one customer base may not hold for ours. I would first build the floor from our own cost per resolved outcome, including retries, failed generations, and the long tail of expensive requests. Then I would compare that floor to the published multiple. If we sit well above it, the rule is a useful sanity check. If we sit below it, I would look for the missing cost first before concluding we are underpriced. The rule only becomes a hard boundary in markets with a standard price that we must match, where the multiple tells us whether we can compete at all.

We'd push back on the premise first, then get Finance to the number they actually need. Full allocation by month end is achievable, but it isn't always the right target. I'd split the cost pool into three buckets: directly attributable spend, shared spend with a usable meter, and shared spend with no defensible driver. The first two get allocated on a schedule, using tags for direct costs and a usage metric such as requests, seats, or GPU-hours for shared costs. For the third bucket, I'd create a named central line with an owner and a review date, and I would not spread it across products just to hit 100 percent, because that charges teams for spend they didn't drive and invites arguments that waste more time than the allocation saves.

For Finance, I'd report two figures each month: allocated coverage as a percentage of total spend, and the central pool with its items listed. I'd track coverage quarter over quarter so the trend shows whether tagging and metering are improving. Where the company's chargeback contract requires full allocation, I'd use a documented proxy for the residual, label those dollars as proxied in every report, and reconcile the total to the invoice so nothing is lost.

Our cloud bill reconciles to the invoice every month, so the allocation is closed and accurate. Coverage above 95 percent is the target we hold teams to, and once we reach it the remaining shared costs are small enough to ignore in product decisions.

I start with the definition, not the price. I find out what ends a conversation, whether silence counts as resolved, what happens when the customer comes back a day later, and whether a handoff to a human ever gets billed. Then I map those rules onto my own contacts so the vendor's unit and mine mean the same thing. Next I pull a random sample of 40 billed resolutions and mark each one resolved, not resolved, or ambiguous, and I count ambiguous as not resolved. Suppose 31 of 40 hold up. My cost per true resolution is 99 cents divided by 0.775, about $1.28, before seat or platform fees. I compare that with what a human-handled ticket costs, using the range rather than the average, and with what the same tickets would cost if I ran them on a token-priced model myself. Cheap means the number beats the human range and the build-your-own option at my accuracy, and I am satisfied the sample is representative. The check I rely on most is sampling, since a sample of 40 is enough to trust the rate at this volume and a spot-check of invoices would not be.

A failed tool log mostly costs us in the input tokens it adds to every later call in the session. In my lab, a 35-line failed log raised the mean input from 137 to 1,184 tokens and the cost per call from $0.000537 to $0.001411, and the agent recovered on the next attempt in the same way it did without the log. In a long session that log gets re-sent and re-billed at every step, so the overhead compounds. My approach would be to keep the error code and the offending output and drop the rest, or to have a cheap model summarise the log once and reuse the summary. I would also check the cache effects, because changing the prefix mid-session breaks a cached read and can wipe out the saving I expected.

By giving the vignettes to people who have not read the checklist and seeing whether they pick the right ones. I would run a reader who has the checklist and a second reader who has only the vignettes, then compare their matches against the answer key of 30 labeled cases. My baseline with no model matched 14 of 30, which tells me the vignettes are solvable by pattern recognition alone, and its misses show where the categories overlap. I would then fix the categories or the wording of the controls, whichever the misses point at, and rerun until the checklist beats the baseline by a clear margin.

A per-product key is the cleaner choice because attribution has to hold up under pressure. If each application sends its own tag in a header, you are trusting every team to spell it correctly, keep it consistent across services, and never copy the wrong value from a template. That fails quietly, and the first time finance asks who owns a line item, the answer is a guess. A key issued per product and bound to an owner at creation means the gateway knows the owner from the credential itself, so the tag cannot be mistyped or forgotten. Headers still have a place for finer detail like the feature or the experiment, and I would keep those, but ownership should always come from the key so the chargeback to a team is trustworthy.

I would not conclude that a dollar cap is free. In this lab it looked cheap because the runs that hit the cap were the long ones, and those were mostly failures anyway, so cutting them removed little value. That result is specific to this agent, one small model, and one synthetic task, with 80 runs per policy. The accuracy differences of 5 to 6 points at the main cap fall inside the noise, so what I can say is that I did not detect a drop there, which is weaker than saying there was none. A cap at half that level does cost accuracy, so the cheap result only holds at or above roughly $0.012 per run. I also did not test a gateway or pre-flight cost estimates, so nothing here transfers to those controls. Before anyone rolls a cap out, I would want to rerun the sweep on production traffic and check the accuracy effect against a pre-set tolerance.

I'd start by mapping the whole cost path before touching the model. For each answer I list every component: the generation call, the retrieved context billed as input tokens, the query embedding, vector store reads, judge sampling, and any human review. Each line gets a unit and a rate, so the sum reconciles to the 25 cents. In the case I have in mind, the model call and retrieval together came to about 0.4 cents, and the human review line was the bulk of the total. That tells you the cheap model was never the problem, and swapping it again would move the number by a fraction of a cent.

Once the stack is visible, the levers are the review rate, the minutes per review, and whether the answer needs review at all. Review rate is the cheapest to test. If it drops from 8 percent to 4 percent, the saving is about 12 cents per answer on average. I'd confirm that by sampling a fixed set of answers at both rates and checking that the quality metric stays at its baseline, which is measured on a labelled set reviewed before the change. Review time is the second lever: if the reviewers are spending eight minutes on answers that a checklist could clear in two, restructuring the review UI cuts cost without touching the sampling rate.

The boundary case is a product where review is mandated, for example by regulation. There the rate is fixed, and the work is entirely on minutes per review and on making the first-pass answer good enough that reviewers confirm rather than rewrite. I'd report the cost per answer alongside the quality metric and the wrong-answer rate so that any saving is visibly paid for by accuracy held constant.

I would start by building the strongest single-agent version of the system and running it on the same task set as the multi-agent design. Then I would compare cost per accepted outcome and wall-clock time, using the same evaluation rubric for both. If the pipeline costs more and delivers neither better accuracy nor a meaningful reduction in latency, the extra complexity is hard to justify. The burden of proof sits with the multi-agent design. Usually it has to rest on a task property the single agent cannot satisfy, such as work that spans more than one context window or needs parallel tool access. Across the six architectures I have seen, a planner, coder and reviewer pipeline cost roughly 3.2 times as much as a single strong call and solved no more tasks in the evaluation. That number is the kind of evidence I would bring to the discussion before anyone adds another agent.

When the label set is stable, volume is high and labelled data exists. One study found fine-tuned encoders beating prompted models on three of four benchmarks at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost at its January 2026 prices. The boundary is a taxonomy that changes often, where retraining erases the saving.

By generating it from the same ledger and the same definitions as everything else, with the assumptions kept in a file the finance director owns, and by reconciling the sum of the units to the invoice. A hand-built page drifts from its source, so the numbers come straight from the pipeline. An agent may draft the commentary text, and a person reads it before it goes out. If a figure on the page cannot be reproduced from the pack's inputs with one command, I would take it off until it can. Every saving we report is tied to the reconciled total, so the story and the ledger always agree.

Run a baseline on a fixed question set, then each lever alone and both together, and log the same usage fields the bill is built from: input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, and request counts. Score quality per question type so a drop in one category doesn't hide inside an average. If the combined saving is larger than the sum of the individual savings, the levers are complementary; if it's smaller, they're competing for the same tokens, so I'd look for the shared prefix or shared output format that both are touching. If quality moves when the pair runs, I'd rerun the lever with the layout change and without it to isolate which change caused the shift.

A budget sets the maximum spend allowed for a given scope and time period, such as a project or team for a month. A quota is essentially a per-user or per-customer budget over a period, so one tenant cannot consume the whole allocation. A kill switch halts spending that is already running, triggered from outside the workload, scoped to a chosen boundary. The first two are preventive and the third is reactive. All three depend on consistent tagging so spend can be attributed, and on a run record showing which jobs are currently in flight. The kill switch in particular should be exercised in a drill before anyone relies on it, since an untested one often fails when needed.

I'd handle it by putting an explicit label on it: the number, its basis, and who owns the assumption, so nobody mistakes it for a measured fact. Then I'd replace it with a measurement as soon as that is cheap. In the pack, the human cost per handoff was an assumption, and the sensitivity table showed it moved the loaded cost by about 2x across the $5 to $10 range, so that is the one I would measure first, with a short timed sample of human-handled tickets. The rework cost moved the total by roughly five percent, so it can wait for a later iteration. Directors tend to remember the headline figure and forget the footnote, so I keep the basis in a visible column next to the number, not buried in an appendix. Once the sample is in, I re-run the model and show the before and after so the change is visible to whoever approved the original figure.

We would bring the acquired company's cloud accounts into our existing cost model as quickly as possible, so that everything reports consistently from day one. I start by inventorying their tags, accounts, and team names, then build a single mapping table that translates their tagging scheme into ours, with each acquired team assigned to a Fieldstone cost center and owner. Once the mapping is in place, I backfill the acquired environment's historical spend into our hierarchy so that trend lines are continuous and year-over-year comparisons work without adjustment. Their products become cost objects under the appropriate parent, and I retire their old tags once the new ones are applied to all resources. Credentials and API keys are rotated onto our gateway in a single cutover window to avoid running two access paths in parallel. I track adoption by confirming that every acquired account shows a complete tag set in the weekly report, and I escalate any account still untagged after the cutover. For a small acquisition this takes a few weeks; for a larger one I would phase the work, but the principle is the same: one model, one set of tags, and history restated so the numbers tell one story.

The check runs at each scope separately: first the team budget, then the project, then the account. For each one it reads the current spend, adds the estimate, and compares the sum to that scope's limit. If every scope has room, the call goes through and the estimate is recorded against all of them. After the call it commits the actual cost and releases the unused portion of the reserve, and on a failed call it releases the reserve entirely. Reporting the scope that blocked the call tells the user which limit to talk about. My class tests that a refusal at one scope leaves no reservation at another, and a production version needs one transaction in a shared store.

When the gateway log shows $100 and the invoice shows $112, my first move is not to change either number. I want to know which fields account for the $12 before I trust either total. At Fieldstone's scale I would sort the difference into three buckets: usage that never passed through the gateway, such as a direct call from a notebook using the vendor key; price mismatches, such as a cache write priced in the table as ordinary input; and charges that aren't tokens at all, such as a reserved-capacity line or a minimum commitment fee. The gateway is a measurement I control, and the invoice is a bill I don't, so the gap usually points to my instrumentation first. I would aim to explain the gap to within two percent of the invoice and assign an owner to whatever remains. The reverse case, a month with a vendor credit where the invoice comes in under the log, gets the same method applied the other way around.

To test a grader on interview answers, I'd start with a paired set: for each question, a strong answer and a plausible-weak answer, presented in both orders so position bias doesn't masquerade as signal. I'd add a truncated version of the strong answer, cut to its core claims but with the same confident tone, to see whether the grader rewards substance or simply length. Then I'd run two or more graders, human and model, over a shared sample and measure agreement, paying closest attention to the pairs where they split, since those disagreements show where the rubric is ambiguous. Finally, I wouldn't treat perfect scores on my own question bank as reassurance. If a grader aces a bank I wrote, that tells me the bank is easy or shares my blind spots, so I'd bring in adversarial items written by someone else before trusting the grader.

A retry is a deliberate repeat of a call after a failure, capped at a fixed number of attempts. A loop is an agent repeating an action, or alternating between two, without changing the state of the task, and it runs indefinitely unless the harness sets a limit. I detect loops from the trace: a repeated action signature, an alternating pair, or a streak of steps adding no new fact. Once a loop is detected, the agent should be stopped immediately and the run killed, because every extra step is wasted spend and the model is clearly not making progress.

I define forecast error as the absolute difference between the forecast and the actual for a stated period, divided by the actual, expressed as a percentage. I always quote the horizon too, meaning how many days before the period the forecast was made, since a 3-day-ahead error and a 60-day-ahead error are not the same thing. Without the horizon the number cannot be compared across models or teams. The definition matters because it decides what the team optimizes. If we measure error against the forecast instead of the actual, the number looks better when spend is growing, and that flatters the model. I also keep the unit explicit, because a monthly total can look accurate while large errors offset each other across products. For a rough sanity check I use simple arithmetic: with spend growing 20 percent a month, a forecast that just carries last month's level forward is already off by about 16.7 percent of the new level. So if a model reports 41 percent error during a growth period, I can separate how much of that is explained by growth alone from what the model actually gets wrong. The metric is most useful when spend moves and least useful for flat, contract-driven spend, where the carry-forward forecast is nearly right anyway and the error figure stops telling us anything about the model.

Attribution coverage is the share of spend that has an owner, measured in dollars. Most teams report the share of cost lines that carry a tag, and that number misleads in a few ways. It counts lines rather than dollars, and the largest lines are often the ones missing tags, so the reported figure looks healthier than the money underneath it. On Fieldstone's October fixture, half the lines are tagged and 40 percent of the dollars are. The number also treats a tag as an owner, when a tag only records that someone applied a label. I report tagged coverage and accepted coverage as separate figures. Tagged coverage is the share of dollars carrying a valid tag, and accepted coverage is the share of dollars whose named owner has confirmed the charge. Accepted coverage stays marked as unknown until the owners sign off, and I track it against an 85 percent threshold for each month's close. The approach holds for a company with one product and one account, where tags are straightforward. It gets harder with shared infrastructure, such as GPU clusters or shared inference endpoints, where allocation rules matter more than tagging completeness.

I start from the product of four numbers: cases, samples per case, judge calls per sample and runs per month. A suite of 1,500 cases, two samples and one judge call each is 3,000 calls a run; at 1,500 tokens in and 150 out on Haiku 4.5 placeholder rates, that is $6.75 a run, and with 40 pull requests a month, $270. I would write the budget in those terms so that anyone who adds a second judge or a larger judge can see the multiplier before merging. To hold the cost down I would run a small smoke set on every pull request and the full suite nightly or on release branches, and I would sample for disagreement, sending to a second judge only the cases where the first judge is unsure. Because the smoke set is a fixed 150 cases, its cost is negligible, so the monthly figure is essentially fixed and the nightly full run is the only number that moves with team size. I would also ask whether the judge has been calibrated against human labels, since a cheap judge that disagrees with people saves nothing. The boundary is a safety-critical product, where suite size is set by risk and the budget follows.
